items.prompt: Define capacity utilisation.
items.canonical_answer: Capacity utilisation is the proportion of its maximum possible output that a business is actually producing in a given period, expressed as a percentage: current output divided by maximum possible output, multiplied by 100.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. No example and no evaluation required.

items.prompt: Explain why a business measures its capacity utilisation.
items.canonical_answer: Because it shows how much of the capacity the business is already paying for is being used, and that governs the fixed cost carried by each unit. Fixed cost per unit is total fixed costs divided by output, so a business using more of its capacity spreads the same rent, finance charges and salaries across more units and its cost per unit falls. The figure is also a warning device: a percentage that is falling month by month shows capacity being paid for and not used, and a percentage close to the limit shows a business with no room to absorb an unexpected order or a breakdown.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose the measure serves must be stated, not only what the measure is.

items.prompt: A fish cannery at Luderitz can process 9 000 cases a week on the shift pattern it works. Last week it processed 6 300 cases. Calculate its capacity utilisation and its spare capacity.
items.canonical_answer:
Capacity utilisation = current output / maximum possible output = 6 300 / 9 000 = 70%.

Spare capacity = maximum capacity - current output = 9 000 - 6 300 = 2 700 cases a week, which is the same gap expressed as 30% of maximum capacity.

At 70% the cannery is carrying a full week of fixed costs on 6 300 cases rather than 9 000, so every case carries more of those costs than it would at full capacity, and there is room for 2 700 cases a week of extra work without buying any more equipment.
marking_guidance: Formula: the formula must be stated before the figures are put into it.
Substitution must be shown, not the answer alone.
Units: every figure carries its currency, its unit of output or its percentage sign.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the figure means for the cannery - the fixed cost carried by each case, or the room left for extra work.
Spare capacity must be given in cases, and the utilisation as a percentage.

items.prompt: A guesthouse in Swakopmund let 936 guest-nights last month, which was 65% of its capacity. Calculate its maximum capacity in guest-nights, and how many more guest-nights it would have had to let to reach 80%.
items.canonical_answer:
Maximum output = current output / capacity utilisation = 936 / 0.65 = 1 440 guest-nights a month.

Output at 80% = capacity utilisation x maximum output = 0.80 x 1 440 = 1 152 guest-nights, so the guesthouse needed 1 152 - 936 = 216 more guest-nights.

The 216 guest-nights are what the target costs in trade, and they are the figure a marketing decision has to deliver; the percentage on its own does not say how much extra business is involved.
marking_guidance: Formula: the formula must be stated before the figures are put into it.
Substitution must be shown, not the answer alone.
Units: every figure carries its currency, its unit of output or its percentage sign.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the extra guest-nights mean for the guesthouse's decision.
The rearranged formula must be used; dividing by a percentage rather than by the decimal is the common slip.

items.prompt: An Otjiwarongo furniture factory could make 1 000 cabinets a month and makes 600, using 20 employees. Explain the difference between its capacity utilisation and its labour productivity.
items.canonical_answer: Capacity utilisation measures output against the maximum output possible, as a percentage; labour productivity measures output against the labour used, as a quantity per worker. The factory's capacity utilisation is 600 out of 1 000, which is 60%, and its labour productivity is 600 / 20 = 30 cabinets per employee a month. They answer different questions and can move apart: if it added 5 employees and output rose to 750 cabinets, capacity utilisation would rise to 75% while productivity stayed at 30 cabinets per employee.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - output against maximum possible output (a percentage) against output per worker (a quantity).
2 marks (AO2): applied to the factory - 60% utilisation and 30 cabinets per employee, and how the two can move apart; 1 mark if only one measure is worked.
Boundary: both measures named in their own units.

items.prompt: A workshop reports capacity utilisation of 58% last year and 74% this year, while the number of units it made and sold is the same in both years. Explain what the change means for the workshop.
items.canonical_answer:
Output is the numerator and maximum capacity the denominator, so if the percentage rose while output stood still, the rise came from the denominator: the workshop's maximum capacity fell. It has closed or mothballed something, cut a shift, or lost staff it has not replaced.

Compared against the sales figure, nothing improved. Compared against cost, something may have: a smaller capacity usually carries smaller fixed costs, so the same output may now be produced more cheaply. What the change does not show is any growth in trade, and it leaves the workshop with less room to take an unexpected order than it had last year.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the percentage must be read against the output figure, and the movement attributed to the numerator or the denominator.
Interpretation: the answer must say what each figure means for the business, not restate it. A rise caused by a smaller denominator is not the same news as a rise caused by more sales.

items.prompt: Explain one reason why a capacity utilisation figure of 95% may not show that a business is performing well.
items.canonical_answer: Because the figure counts output produced, not output sold. A business can hold the percentage at 95% by producing into stock, so the plant looks fully used while the goods sit in a warehouse. Cash that was spent on materials and wages is tied up in inventory instead of coming back as sales revenue, and if the goods are eventually sold at a discount, or not sold at all, the high percentage will have been bought at a loss. The figure needs reading beside the sales figure and the level of finished stock before it means anything about performance.
marking_guidance: Developed: the limitation must be carried through to an effect on the business, because a named drawback on its own is not developed.
The answer must identify what the measure leaves out, and follow that through to a consequence for the business.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which a fall in output raises a manufacturer's cost per unit.
items.canonical_answer: The fixed costs of a period - rent, finance charges, insurance, the salaries of permanent staff - are a total that does not follow output within the period. Fixed cost per unit is that total divided by output, so when output falls the same total is divided between fewer units and each unit carries more of it. Variable cost per unit is not affected, because materials and the wages paid for each unit made fall with the number of units. Total cost per unit is the sum of the two, so it rises by exactly the amount by which fixed cost per unit rises. At an unmoved selling price, the profit earned on each unit falls by the same amount.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must say how the cause produces the effect, not only that it does.
The answer must separate the behaviour of fixed cost per unit from that of variable cost per unit.

items.prompt: A dairy can bottle 40 000 litres a month and has fixed costs of N$96 000 a month. Calculate its capacity utilisation and its fixed cost per litre at an output of 24 000 litres, and again at 32 000 litres.
items.canonical_answer:
At 24 000 litres: capacity utilisation = 24 000 / 40 000 = 60%, and fixed cost per litre = total fixed costs / output = 96 000 / 24 000 = N$4.00.

At 32 000 litres: capacity utilisation = 32 000 / 40 000 = 80%, and fixed cost per litre = 96 000 / 32 000 = N$3.00.

Twenty percentage points of extra capacity utilisation take N$4.00 - N$3.00 = N$1.00 of fixed cost off every litre the dairy bottles. Nothing has become cheaper to buy; the same N$96 000 is simply being carried by 8 000 more litres.
marking_guidance: Formula: the formula must be stated before the figures are put into it.
Substitution must be shown, not the answer alone.
Units: every figure carries its currency, its unit of output or its percentage sign.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the fall in fixed cost per litre means for the dairy, in N$ per litre.
Capacity utilisation is a percentage and fixed cost per litre is a currency amount; the two must not be confused.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a business of deliberately holding some spare capacity.
items.canonical_answer: It can accept an unexpected order without paying a premium to fill it. A business running at its limit that receives a large enquiry has to turn it down, quote a delivery date far enough ahead to lose the customer, or buy the extra output through overtime, hired equipment or a subcontractor, all of which cost more per unit than normal production. A business with spare capacity takes the order at its ordinary cost, so the whole of the contribution on it is added to profit, and it keeps a customer that would otherwise have gone elsewhere. The spare capacity is not free - it is fixed cost being carried by fewer units - so the benefit is worth having where enquiries of that kind are frequent enough to cover that cost.
marking_guidance: Developed: the benefit must be carried through to an effect on the business, because a named advantage on its own is not developed.
The answer must price the benefit against the cost of the spare capacity, because unused capacity is itself an expense.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a furniture factory of demand rising above the level its plant can produce at normal working.
items.canonical_answer:
The starting condition is that the plant is already at the output its machines, floor space and shift pattern were designed for, and the order book is above it.

The factory then has three answers short of investing, and each carries a cost. If it turns work away, it gives up the contribution those orders would have earned and the buyer may place the work with a competitor who can deliver, which costs future orders as well as this one. If it quotes a longer lead time, the same thing can happen more slowly. If it buys the extra output - overtime at a premium, a weekend shift, or a subcontractor - the output arrives but at a higher cost per unit than the same units made at normal rates, so the contribution on the extra work is thinner than on the rest.

Holding the plant at that level also removes the slack the factory used for servicing and for training. Machines run longer between services, so an unplanned breakdown becomes more likely, and a breakdown removes more output than the service would have done. Staff on sustained overtime tend to make more mistakes, so reworking and returns are likely to rise.

The effect on the business is therefore a smaller gain in profit than the extra sales suggest, together with a rising risk to delivery reliability and to the reputation the factory sells on. Whether the extra demand is worth meeting at all turns on how long it is expected to last: a peak of a few weeks is worth buying output for, while demand that stays above capacity is a case for more capacity rather than for permanent overtime.
marking_guidance: Condition: the plant must be at its designed limit before the chain starts.
Mechanism: the answer must say why the effect follows, not assert it.  Each of the three responses must be traced, not listed.
Consequence: the consequence must include both the cost of the extra output and the effect of losing slack.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and its reliability to customers.

items.prompt: A bakery has run at 97% of capacity for six months, and over the same period the proportion of its deliveries returned by shops has risen from 1% to 4%. Explain what the two figures together mean for the bakery.
items.canonical_answer:
Read alone, 97% looks like an efficient operation: the ovens are almost fully used and the bakery's fixed costs are spread across close to the largest output it can make.

Read against the returns figure, it looks like an operation running without slack. Returns have risen by three percentage points, which is four times the earlier rate, over exactly the period the bakery has been at its limit. At that level there is no time for servicing between runs, no room to slow a line that is producing poorly, and checks are the easiest thing to shorten when a delivery has to leave.

So the two figures together suggest the bakery is buying its high utilisation with quality. The cost of a returned delivery falls on the bakery twice - the goods are wasted and the shop's confidence is damaged - so the right comparison is the extra contribution earned by the last few percentage points of capacity against the cost of the returns they are producing.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the utilisation figure must be read against the returns figure, and both against the earlier period.
Interpretation: the answer must say what each figure means for the business, not restate it. A high percentage bought at the cost of quality is not the same result as a high percentage without it.

context.situation: sustained operation at the capacity limit

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a small engineering workshop should aim to run at 100% of its capacity throughout the year.
items.canonical_answer:
It should not. It should aim for a high utilisation with a deliberate margin below the limit - something in the region of 85 to 90% for a workshop of this kind - rather than for 100%.

The decisive criterion is what the last few percentage points of capacity cost to obtain and to hold. A workshop at 100% has no window for servicing its machines and no cover for absence, so a single breakdown or one skilled fitter off sick removes output it has no way of replacing, and the orders affected are late. It also has nothing to offer a customer who arrives with urgent work, which in engineering is often the profitable work. The fixed cost saved by the last few points of utilisation is small, because most of the fall in fixed cost per unit has already happened by the time the workshop is near its limit.

The strongest argument the other way is real: capacity that is not used is still being paid for, and a small workshop with a thin margin cannot afford to carry much of it. A business whose work is steady, whose machines are reliable and whose customers order well in advance loses little by running at the limit, and gains the lowest cost per unit available to it.

That is the condition on the judgement. Where demand is predictable and orders are placed ahead, a target close to the limit is defensible. Where work arrives at short notice, where breakdowns have been frequent, or where the workshop depends on a few skilled people, the margin is worth more than the cost of holding it, and the answer changes.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must be argued for a small engineering workshop, where one machine and one skilled worker matter.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named.  The decisive factor is what the last few percentage points of capacity cost to hold, against the fixed cost they save.
Counterargument: the strongest argument against the recommendation must be met.  Unused capacity is paid for whether it is used or not, and a small business with a thin margin feels that.
Condition: the judgement must name what would reverse it - predictable demand and orders placed well ahead, or the opposite.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to treat 100% capacity utilisation as the best position for a business to be in?
items.canonical_answer: Because 100% is the lowest fixed cost per unit and nothing else. It buys that figure by removing all slack. There is no window in which machines can be serviced, so deferred servicing makes an unplanned breakdown more likely; there is no cover for absence; there is no room for an unexpected order except by paying a premium for overtime or a subcontractor; and quality checks are the first thing shortened when a delivery has to leave. A business at 100% for a week is in a different position from one at 100% for a year. The sensible target is a high utilisation with a margin, and how large a margin depends on how predictable the business's demand and its equipment are.
marking_guidance: The answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is.
Credit the point that 100% removes the slack used for maintenance, absence cover and unexpected orders.

items.prompt: A brickworks can fire 180 000 bricks a month and currently fires 117 000. Calculate the extra monthly output it would need to reach 85% capacity utilisation.
items.canonical_answer:
Output at 85% = capacity utilisation x maximum output = 0.85 x 180 000 = 153 000 bricks a month.

Extra output needed = 153 000 - 117 000 = 36 000 bricks a month.

Present utilisation is 117 000 / 180 000 = 65%, so reaching 85% means selling 36 000 more bricks a month, which is 36 000 / 117 000 = 31% more than the brickworks sells now. That percentage, rather than the twenty-point rise in utilisation, is the size of the marketing task.
marking_guidance: Formula: the formula must be stated before the figures are put into it.
Substitution must be shown, not the answer alone.
Units: every figure carries its currency, its unit of output or its percentage sign.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the extra output means for the brickworks, expressed as a percentage rise on present sales.
The answer must be in bricks a month, not in percentage points.

items.prompt: Analyse how reducing its price could raise a bottling plant's capacity utilisation, and what the business gives up by choosing that method.
items.canonical_answer:
The starting condition is that the plant has idle capacity and that its market is sensitive enough to price for a cut to bring extra buyers.

A lower price raises the quantity demanded, so more crates are filled and capacity utilisation rises. Because the fixed costs of the period do not move with output, the same total is spread across more crates and fixed cost per crate falls, which is the gain the plant is after.

What it gives up is contribution on every crate, including the crates it was already selling at the old price. If the price falls by N$11 on a crate that was contributing N$48, contribution becomes N$37, so the plant needs the total contribution to be rebuilt out of volume: dividing the contribution it earns now by N$37 gives the number of crates required simply to stand still. Below that volume the higher utilisation is bought at a lower profit than before.

The effect on the business therefore depends on how much extra volume the cut actually brings. A price-sensitive market can leave the plant fuller and more profitable; a market that responds weakly leaves it fuller and poorer, and a competitor matching the cut can leave it with the same share at a lower margin. There is also a longer effect on customers, who may resist a return to the old price.
marking_guidance: Condition: the market must be price-sensitive for the chain to start, and the plant must have idle capacity.
Mechanism: the answer must say why the effect follows, not assert it.  The loss of contribution on units already being sold must be part of the reasoning.
Consequence: the consequence must include the volume needed simply to earn the same total contribution.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and the position it leaves with customers and competitors.

items.prompt: A campsite near Sesriem is fully booked for four months of the year and about one-fifth occupied for the other eight. Its owner will not reduce the number of pitches, because the busy season fills all of them. Explain one method of raising its capacity utilisation that fits those circumstances.
items.canonical_answer:
Because the owner will not cut capacity and the peak already fills it, the only route left is to raise demand in the eight quiet months, and the method has to reach buyers who travel then. Offering reduced off-season rates to school and university groups, tour operators running domestic trips, and conference or training parties targets exactly that gap: those buyers choose their dates for price and availability rather than for the season, which is why they are reachable when the campsite is one-fifth full and not when it is full.

The site's fixed costs - the lease, the ablution blocks, the permanent staff - are being paid through all twelve months, so any off-season booking that covers the cost of servicing a pitch adds to covering them. The method also fits the owner's constraint, because it raises the numerator without touching the pitches the peak season needs.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the campsite's own facts - a four-month peak that fills capacity, eight quiet months, and an owner who will not cut pitches.
Reasoning: the method must be shown to work because of those facts, not in general.
Conclusion: one named method must be reached, and it must be one the owner's constraint allows.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of rationalisation as a method of raising capacity utilisation.
items.canonical_answer: It is slow and expensive to reverse. Cutting capacity means selling or mothballing equipment, giving up floor space and making staff redundant, and each of those is easier to do than to undo. A business that reduces capacity and then finds demand recovering has to order equipment and wait for delivery and installation, recruit and train replacement staff, and take back floor space at whatever rent is then being asked, so it may be unable to supply the recovered demand for months. In the meantime the orders it cannot fill are available to competitors that kept their capacity. That is why rationalisation suits a fall in demand judged to be permanent, and why a business facing a fall it thinks temporary is usually better served by reducing the capacity it uses rather than the capacity it owns.
marking_guidance: Developed: the limitation must be carried through to an effect on the business, because a named drawback on its own is not developed.
The limitation must be tied to the reversibility of the decision and followed through to what the business loses if demand returns.

items.prompt: Why is a rise in capacity utilisation not by itself evidence that a business is doing better?
items.canonical_answer: Because the percentage can rise for two quite different reasons. Output can rise, which is normally good news, or maximum capacity can fall, which is not news of the same kind: a business that closes a line raises the figure without selling one extra unit. And even a rise driven by output is only worth having if the output is sold. A business producing into a warehouse it cannot empty raises the percentage while tying up cash in inventory and carrying the risk that the goods go unsold. The figure has to be read beside output, sales and the level of finished stock before it says anything about performance.
marking_guidance: The answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is.
Both routes to a higher percentage must appear: a larger numerator and a smaller denominator.

items.prompt: A Windhoek retailer is considering paying a Windhoek courier to run its deliveries, and a Namibian bank is considering opening its own processing office in another country. Explain the difference between outsourcing and offshoring, using these two plans.
items.canonical_answer: Outsourcing is about who performs an activity - it is handed to another business; offshoring is about where it is performed - it is moved to another country. The retailer's plan is outsourcing without offshoring: the deliveries go to another business, but they stay in Windhoek. The bank's plan is offshoring without outsourcing: the work moves abroad, but the office is still part of the bank. The two are independent, and a business that handed its call centre to a firm in another country would be doing both.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - who performs the activity against where it is performed.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the two plans - one of each without the other; 1 mark if only one plan is classified.
Boundary: both sides of the difference given; the two are independent.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a business already at full capacity of outsourcing part of its production.
items.canonical_answer: It can supply the extra demand without committing capital to capacity it may not need for long. Buying a machine to meet a surge means paying for that machine for years, and if the surge does not last the business is left carrying fixed costs on equipment that stands idle, which raises the fixed cost carried by every unit it does make. Placing the overflow with a supplier is paid for by the unit of work used, so the cost appears only while the extra demand does and stops when it stops. The business keeps the sales and the contribution on them, and its own plant continues at the output it was designed for. Capacity bought this way can also usually start sooner than capacity that has to be ordered, delivered and installed.
marking_guidance: Developed: the benefit must be carried through to an effect on the business, because a named advantage on its own is not developed.
The benefit must be tied to the business being at its capacity limit, because that is what makes the alternative a capital decision.

items.prompt: A printer binds 3 000 books a month in-house. Materials and labour come to N$46 a book. The binding line costs N$54 000 a month to run, and the whole of that N$54 000 would end if the line closed, because its floor space is separately leased and can be given up and its operator works on nothing else. A supplier quotes N$70 a book. Calculate which is cheaper at 3 000 books a month, and the monthly volume at which the two cost the same.
items.canonical_answer:
In-house total cost = (variable cost per book x output) + avoidable fixed cost = 46 x 3 000 = N$138 000, and 138 000 + 54 000 = N$192 000 a month, which is 192 000 / 3 000 = N$64 a book.

Outsourced total cost = 70 x 3 000 = N$210 000 a month.

In-house is cheaper by 210 000 - 192 000 = N$18 000 a month.

The two cost the same where the supplier's higher price per book has absorbed the whole of the avoidable fixed cost. The difference per book is 70 - 46 = N$24, so the volume at which they are equal is 54 000 / 24 = 2 250 books a month.

Above 2 250 books the printer is cheaper binding in-house, because the N$54 000 is spread across enough books to bring the in-house cost per book below N$70; below 2 250 the supplier is cheaper. At 3 000 books the printer should keep the work, and the figure to watch is its monthly volume, not the quotation.
marking_guidance: Formula: the formula must be stated before the figures are put into it.
Substitution must be shown, not the answer alone.
Units: every figure carries its currency, its unit of output or its percentage sign.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the break-even volume means for the printer's decision.
Only the avoidable fixed cost belongs in the in-house figure, and the prompt states that the whole N$54 000 is avoidable.
The equal-cost volume must be in books a month.

facts: line cost N$54 000 a month, all avoidable

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of outsourcing an activity that a business's customers judge it by.
items.canonical_answer: The business loses direct control over the activity while keeping the consequences of it going wrong. A supplier schedules the work to suit its own operation and its other clients, so an urgent job competes with everyone else's, and the business hears about a failure when its own customer complains rather than when the problem arises. Because the customer bought from the business, the damaged reputation is the business's and not the supplier's, and repeat orders are lost to it. A contract can set standards and penalties, but a penalty returns money and does not return the customer. That is why the limitation bites hardest exactly where the activity is one customers choose the business for, and barely at all where they never see it.
marking_guidance: Developed: the limitation must be carried through to an effect on the business, because a named drawback on its own is not developed.
The answer must separate what is transferred - the work - from what is not, which is responsibility to the customer.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a food manufacturer of outsourcing the production of a component it has made for itself for many years.
items.canonical_answer:
The starting condition is that the manufacturer closes its own capability: the equipment is sold, the floor space given up and the staff who ran it redeployed or made redundant. That is what makes the cost avoidable, and it is also what makes the step hard to undo.

The immediate effect is on cost and cash. The avoidable fixed cost ends and the component is bought by the unit, so the manufacturer's fixed costs fall and its costs move with its output. Where the supplier's price is below the avoidable in-house cost at the volume it actually makes, cost per unit falls as well.

The effect over the life of the contract runs the other way. Because the equipment and the people have gone, bringing the work back would mean buying equipment again and rebuilding the skill, which takes months. The supplier is aware of that, so at renewal the manufacturer negotiates from a weaker position than it held at the start and the price may be raised. How far that goes depends on how many other suppliers could make the component: several capable ones and the manufacturer can move; one and it cannot.

There is a second effect where the component is part of what the manufacturer competes on. Making it teaches the supplier the recipe or the specification, and the supplier may sell to the manufacturer's competitors or enter the market itself, so a difference the manufacturer relied on may narrow.

The effect on the business is therefore lower cost now against a weaker bargaining position and, where the component is distinctive, a thinner competitive advantage later. Which dominates depends on how much cost was genuinely avoidable and on whether the component is one customers buy the product for.
marking_guidance: Condition: the in-house capability must actually be closed for the chain to start, which is what makes the cost avoidable.
Mechanism: the answer must say why the effect follows, not assert it.  The weakening of the bargaining position must be explained through the cost of rebuilding the capability.
Consequence: the consequence must cover both the cost saved now and the price risk at renewal.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and its competitive position.

items.prompt: A Windhoek accountancy practice of twelve people spends about six hours a week of a qualified accountant's time on its own bookkeeping, payroll and computer problems. Explain why outsourcing that work may suit it.
items.canonical_answer:
The six hours are the point. They are hours of a qualified accountant, and the practice sells those hours to clients, so every hour spent on its own payroll or on a failed printer is an hour of chargeable work not done. Buying the same work from a bookkeeping firm and an IT contractor returns those six hours a week to fee-earning, and in a practice of twelve people there is no one else qualified to absorb them.

The activities also suit being bought in. None of them is what clients choose this practice for, so handing them over gives nothing away. Each is a standard service with several providers in Windhoek, so the practice is not tied to one supplier, and the standard required can be written down and checked. A specialist payroll firm handling many employers also follows changes in the rules as part of its own business, which a twelve-person practice has to do in the same six hours.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the practice's own facts - twelve people, six hours a week, and the time being a qualified accountant's.
Reasoning: the opportunity cost of those hours must drive the argument, because that is what the facts change.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a clear statement that the work suits being outsourced, and say which work.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a Namibian clothing manufacturer should outsource the cutting and sewing of its garments to a supplier in another country while keeping its design work in-house.
items.canonical_answer:
On balance it should not outsource the whole of cutting and sewing, and if it outsources at all it should place only its plainest, highest-volume lines and keep the rest.

The decisive criterion is how close cutting and sewing sit to what customers buy the garments for. Design is what the manufacturer intends to keep, but a design is realised in the making: the fit, the finish and the consistency of the stitching are what a buyer judges, and those are decided by the people cutting and sewing. Handing that over means the manufacturer keeps the drawings and loses control of the article, while remaining the business its customers hold responsible for a poor garment. A supplier abroad adds distance to the problem: a fault is discovered after the goods have travelled, and correcting it costs a shipment rather than a morning.

The argument for outsourcing is strong and should not be dismissed. A supplier running cutting and sewing for many customers may hold equipment and a wage cost no Namibian manufacturer of this size can match, and the saving is real wherever the factory, machines and operators here would genuinely be given up. Against that, the saving has to be measured against avoidable cost only, and has to carry freight, duty, the cost of inspecting what arrives, and exposure to exchange-rate movements where the supplier prices in its own currency.

The judgement changes on two conditions. If the supplier will work to a written specification with inspection before shipment, and the lines placed are ones that never carry the design work the manufacturer competes on, then the cost argument can be allowed to decide. And if several suppliers can do the work, so the manufacturer can move if quality slips, the dependence risk is smaller and more of the range can be placed outside.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must be argued for a manufacturer whose design is its selling point and whose supplier would be in another country.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named.  The decisive factor is how close cutting and sewing sit to what customers buy the garments for.
Counterargument: the strongest argument against the recommendation must be met.  A specialist supplier's cost advantage is genuine and has to be met rather than dismissed.
Condition: the judgement must name what would change it - an inspected written specification, plain high-volume lines, or several available suppliers.

context.situation: considering placing production abroad while keeping design
facts: cutting and sewing would go to a supplier abroad

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume that outsourcing an activity reduces a business's total costs?
items.canonical_answer: Because the comparison that matters is not the supplier's price against the recorded in-house cost. It is the supplier's price against the in-house cost that is genuinely avoidable - the spending that would actually stop if the activity stopped. A recorded in-house cost normally includes a share of overheads that continue whatever happens: a factory lease with years to run, a manager who also does other work, insurance on a building the business keeps. Those are unavoidable over the period in question, so the supplier's price is added to them rather than replacing them, and total cost rises even though the comparison appeared to show a saving. The costs of running the contract - specifying the work, inspecting what arrives, moving goods - belong on the supplier's side of the comparison as well.
marking_guidance: The answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is.
Credit the distinction between recorded in-house cost and avoidable in-house cost.

items.prompt: Kunene Tanning treats 5 400 hides a month at a plant that can treat 9 000. Its fixed costs are N$594 000 a month. Each hide costs N$85 in chemicals, water and direct labour, and the plant incurs no other cost that varies with the number of hides treated; treated hides sell for N$260. A footwear manufacturer offers a standing order for a further 2 700 hides a month at N$180 each on a one-year contract, and the tannery has no other enquiries for the idle capacity. Calculate the present capacity utilisation, the present monthly profit, and what each becomes if the order is taken, and evaluate whether Kunene should accept it.
items.canonical_answer:
Now. Capacity utilisation = 5 400 / 9 000 = 60%. Contribution per hide = 260 - 85 = N$175, so monthly contribution = 175 x 5 400 = N$945 000 and monthly profit = 945 000 - 594 000 = N$351 000. Fixed cost per hide = 594 000 / 5 400 = N$110.00.

With the order. Output = 5 400 + 2 700 = 8 100 hides, so capacity utilisation = 8 100 / 9 000 = 90%. The extra hides contribute 180 - 85 = N$95 each, which is 95 x 2 700 = N$256 500 a month, so profit becomes 351 000 + 256 500 = N$607 500. Fixed cost per hide falls to 594 000 / 8 100 = N$73.33, because the same fixed total is carried by 2 700 more hides.

Judgement: accept the order. The decisive criterion is that the capacity is otherwise idle and has no other enquiry against it, so the N$180 price does not have to cover the fixed costs - those are being paid at 5 400 hides already. It only has to cover the N$85 the extra hides cost to treat, and it covers it by N$95 a hide, which is N$256 500 a month of contribution the tannery would not otherwise have.

The strongest argument against is the length and the price of the commitment. N$180 is well below the N$260 the tannery charges, and a one-year standing order fills 30 percentage points of capacity that cannot then be released if a full-price customer appears. If a buyer at N$260 arrived for those same 2 700 hides, the contract would be costing Kunene 260 - 180 = N$80 a hide, which is 80 x 2 700 = N$216 000 a month of contribution given up.

The judgement is therefore conditional on the state of the market for the year ahead. It holds while full-price demand is not expected to recover to 8 100 hides within the contract, and while the N$180 can be treated as a contract price for this buyer rather than a rate other customers can ask for. If either fails, the answer is to take a shorter contract or a smaller volume.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must recommend a course of action rather than present both sides and stop.

Context: the recommendation must rest on the facts of the business given, not on the issue in the abstract.  the recommendation must rest on Kunene's own idle capacity and the absence of other enquiries.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named.  The decisive factor is that the fixed costs are being paid at 5 400 hides regardless, so the N$180 has only the N$85 to cover.

Counterargument: the strongest argument against must be met, not listed.  A one-year commitment at N$180 against a list price of N$260 blocks capacity for a full-price buyer, and the contribution given up must be calculated rather than asserted.
Condition: the answer must end on what would change the judgement.  The answer must end on what would reverse it - full-price demand returning, or the price becoming visible to other customers.
All six figures must be calculated with the working shown.

context.situation: a below-list standing order for idle capacity
facts: no other enquiries for the idle capacity

items.prompt: Namib Dairy Foods delivers to 140 shops from nine refrigerated vans of its own. Running the fleet costs N$918 000 a year in wages, fuel, licences and maintenance, all of which would end if the fleet were sold, and the vans would fetch about N$1 200 000. A national logistics firm offers to take the deliveries for N$6 300 a shop a year on a three-year contract. Two of the dairy's largest customers have said that same-day replacement of a damaged delivery is the reason they buy from it. Analyse the circumstances in which Namib Dairy Foods should outsource its distribution, and evaluate what it should do.
items.canonical_answer:
The numbers first. Outsourced cost = 6 300 x 140 = N$882 000 a year, against N$918 000 in-house, so the saving is 918 000 - 882 000 = N$36 000 a year, which is 36 000 / 918 000 = 4% of what the fleet costs to run. Selling the vans would also release about N$1 200 000 of cash.

It should outsource where three things hold: the cost genuinely avoidable in-house is above the contract price by a margin worth the disruption, the service standard customers judge the dairy by can be written into the contract and checked, and enough alternative carriers exist that the dairy can move at renewal. It should keep the work where the service is itself part of what customers buy, because a carrier scheduling for many clients cannot give one client's emergency priority without being paid to.

Recommendation: do not hand over the whole operation. The decisive factor is that the saving is N$36 000 a year - 4% - while the capability being handed over is the one two of the dairy's largest customers name as their reason for buying. A saving of that size does not justify placing that service in the hands of a firm whose schedule the dairy does not control: for the saving to be worth making, the whole annual contribution from those two customers would have to be smaller than N$36 000, and two of the dairy's largest customers are not that small.

The strongest argument the other way is the N$1 200 000 tied up in vans. That is real money doing nothing in a dairy business, and a fleet also carries risks - accidents, breakdowns, drivers - that a dairy has no particular skill in managing. The answer to it is a split rather than a refusal: place the routine long routes to outlying shops with the logistics firm, and keep three or four vans for the customers who need same-day replacement. That releases part of the capital and part of the cost while keeping the service that sells.

The recommendation reverses if the logistics firm will contract to a same-day replacement standard with a named service level and a penalty that reflects the value of the customer, or if the dairy has a use for the N$1 200 000 that earns more than the risk costs. It would also change if a second carrier appeared, because the three-year term is long for a market with one credible supplier in it.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must recommend a course of action rather than present both sides and stop.

Context: the recommendation must rest on the facts of the business given, not on the issue in the abstract.  the recommendation must use the dairy's own facts - 140 shops, N$36 000 of saving, and the two customers who named same-day replacement.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named.  The decisive factor is the size of the saving measured against the customer relationships it puts at risk.
Counterargument: the strongest argument against must be met, not listed.  The N$1 200 000 released by selling the vans is a serious argument for outsourcing and must be answered, not ignored.

Condition: the answer must end on what would change the judgement.  The answer must name what would reverse it - a contracted service level with a meaningful penalty, or another carrier entering the market.
Both the circumstances for outsourcing and the circumstances against must be analysed before the recommendation is made.

quotation N$6 300 a shop a year
two large customers value same-day replacement

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Otavi Cement has run at 44% of capacity for two years since a large construction customer was lost. Its fixed costs are N$14 400 000 a year, and mothballing one of its two kilns would take N$4 800 000 a year out of that figure while halving capacity. A government road-building programme has been announced that may begin within eighteen months. Evaluate whether Otavi should mothball the kiln.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: mothball the kiln only on terms that keep it recoverable - preserve the kiln rather than sell it, and keep enough of the crew to restart - unless the road programme can be confirmed with orders rather than announcements, in which case wait.

Paragraph 1 - what 44% is costing now. The N$14 400 000 is being carried by a little over two-fifths of the output the plant was built for, so fixed cost per tonne is more than twice what it would be at full capacity, and every tonne Otavi sells is priced against competitors who may not be carrying that burden.

Paragraph 2 - what mothballing does to the figures. It removes N$4 800 000 a year of fixed cost and halves maximum capacity, so at the same output capacity utilisation moves from 44% to 88% while the fixed total falls to 14 400 000 - 4 800 000 = N$9 600 000, which takes a third off fixed cost per tonne. The percentage doubles without a single extra tonne being sold, which is why the gain to argue about is the N$4 800 000, not the percentage.

Paragraph 3 - the case against acting now. Cement capacity is slow and expensive to restore: a mothballed kiln has to be recommissioned, and a dispersed crew has to be recruited and trained. If the road programme begins within eighteen months Otavi could be unable to supply it, and the orders would go to a competitor that kept its capacity - which is a permanent loss of position, not a temporary one.

Paragraph 4 - weighing the two. Two years at 44% is evidence that the lost demand has not returned on its own, and an announced programme is not an order. The cost of waiting is N$4 800 000 a year; the cost of acting wrongly is the road contracts.

Judgement and conditions: mothball rather than dismantle, keep a core crew, and set the decision to be revisited when the programme's first tenders are issued. Reverse to full capacity on firm orders, not on the announcement. Move to permanent closure only if the eighteen months pass without them.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must recommend a course of action rather than present both sides and stop.

Context: the recommendation must rest on the facts of the business given, not on the issue in the abstract.  the plan must use Otavi's own facts - 44% for two years, N$4 800 000 of fixed cost, an announced but unstarted programme.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named.  The decisive factor is the cost of carrying the idle kiln measured against the cost of being unable to supply the road programme.
Counterargument: the strongest argument against must be met, not listed.  The strongest case for waiting - that recovering cement capacity is slow - must be met rather than listed.
Condition: the answer must end on what would change the judgement.  The plan must end on what would change the answer: firm tenders rather than an announcement.
A plan is what is assessed here: the structure and the point at which the judgement is reached, not continuous prose.

context.situation: prolonged under-utilisation with a possible recovery in prospect
facts: mothballing saves N$4 800 000 a year and halves capacity

items.prompt: A bank is considering a loan application from a manufacturer whose business plan reports capacity utilisation of 88%. Identify the questions the bank should ask about that figure before relying on it, and explain what each one would tell it.
items.canonical_answer:
How is maximum capacity defined? The denominator follows the shift pattern assumed, the maintenance time allowed and the product mix. A maximum stated on a one-shift basis makes 88% out of an output that would be 44% on two shifts, so the bank needs the basis before the figure means anything.

Was the output sold, or produced? The measure counts output, not sales. If finished stock has risen over the period, part of that 88% is inventory rather than trade, and the cash the bank is being asked to lend against is sitting in a warehouse.

What does the figure look like over time? One period tells the bank nothing about direction. Three years of monthly figures show whether 88% is a recovery, a plateau or the top of a fall.

What is the maintenance and quality record at that level? A plant held near its limit tends to defer servicing and shorten checks, so a rising level of returns or breakdowns beside a high percentage is a warning that the figure is being bought rather than earned.

What happens to the plan if demand grows? At 88% there is 12% of headroom. If the plan's revenue forecast needs more output than that, the business is forecasting sales it cannot make without overtime, a subcontractor or capital spending, and each of those changes the cost forecast the bank is reading.

How does it compare with the industry? A utilisation that looks high in one industry is ordinary in another, so the bank needs a comparison with businesses measuring capacity on the same basis before it treats 88% as a strength.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Reason: each question must carry the reason it matters - what a poor answer would mean for the figure.
Context: these are questions a bank asks about a plan, so each must bear on whether the business can repay, not on operations for their own sake.

context.situation: a lender reviewing a business plan
